{{Short description|Theory in probability theory}}
In [[probability theory]], the '''Feldman–Hájek theorem''' or '''Feldman–Hájek dichotomy''' is a fundamental result in the theory of [[Gaussian measure]]s.  It states that two Gaussian measures <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> on a [[locally convex space]] <math>X</math> are either [[equivalent measures]] or else [[singular measure|mutually singular]]:<ref name="Bogachev">{{cite book
| last = Bogachev
| first = Vladimir I.
| title = Gaussian Measures
| series = Mathematical Surveys and Monographs
| volume = 62
| publisher = American Mathematical Society
| location = Providence, RI
| year = 1998
| isbn = 0-8218-1054-5
| doi = 10.1090/surv/062}} (See Theorem 2.7.2)</ref>  there is no possibility of an intermediate situation in which, for example, <math>\mu</math> has a [[probability density function|density]] with respect to <math>\nu</math> but not vice versa.  In the special case that <math>X</math> is a [[Hilbert space]], it is possible to give an explicit description of the circumstances under which <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> are equivalent:  writing <math>m_{\mu}</math> and <math>m_{\nu}</math> for the means of <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu,</math> and <math>C_\mu</math> and <math>C_\nu</math> for their [[covariance operator]]s, equivalence of <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> holds if and only if<ref name="DaPratoZabczyk">{{cite book
| last1 = Da Prato
| first1 = Giuseppe
| last2 = Zabczyk
| first2 = Jerzy
| title = Stochastic Equations in Infinite Dimensions
| series = Encyclopedia of Mathematics and its Applications
| volume = 152
| edition = Second
| publisher = Cambridge University Press
| location = Cambridge
| year = 2014
| isbn = 978-1-107-05584-1
| doi = 10.1017/CBO9781107295513}} (See Theorem 2.25)</ref>
* <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math> have the same [[Cameron–Martin theorem|Cameron–Martin space]] <math>H = C_\mu^{1/2}(X) = C_\nu^{1/2}(X)</math>;
* the difference in their means lies in this common Cameron–Martin space, i.e. <math>m_\mu - m_\nu \in H</math>;  and
* the operator <math>(C_\mu^{-1/2} C_\nu^{1/2}) (C_\mu^{-1/2} C_\nu^{1/2})^{\ast} - I</math> is a [[Hilbert–Schmidt operator]] on <math>\bar{H}.</math>

A simple consequence of the Feldman–Hájek theorem is that dilating a Gaussian measure on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space <math>X</math> (i.e. taking <math>C_\nu = s C_\mu</math> for some scale factor <math>s \geq 0</math>) always yields two mutually singular Gaussian measures, except for the trivial dilation with <math>s = 1,</math> since <math>(s^2 - 1) I</math> is Hilbert–Schmidt only when <math>s = 1.</math>
